summary: The Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5% and warns more may come as oil keeps prices high, and Carney hosts EU leaders in Montréal to start talks on a closer alliance.
body: The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate on Wednesday by a quarter point to 2.5%, its first increase since 2023 [^1][^2]. It said inflation is higher and more stubborn than it expected in July: prices have risen about 3% a year since April and could reach about 3.5% by year-end, mostly because of high oil prices during the eighth month of the Middle East conflict [^1]. Without gasoline, inflation was 2.2% in September [^1]. Governor Tiff Macklem said the hike is meant to stop high energy costs from spilling into other prices, and the bank warned there "could be a need" to raise rates again [^1][^2]. The next decision is December 9 [^1].

What it means at home: people with variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit feel a hike first [^2]. The bank expects the economy to grow just 1% this year, slowed by new US tariffs, with unemployment around 6.5% [^1]. Economist Trevor Tombe estimated for The Hub that high oil prices could cost the average household about $500 a year at the pump and another $500 in food, flights and other energy-linked goods [^2].

Today and Friday, Prime Minister Mark Carney hosts EU leaders Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa in Montréal, ten years after the Canada-EU trade deal was signed [^3]. They plan to launch talks on an "Alliance for the Future" covering trade, defence, critical minerals, technology and research, possibly including Canadian students joining the EU's Erasmus+ exchange program [^3][^4]. Von der Leyen has floated "associate" membership, a status that does not exist in EU law; Carney has ruled out joining the EU and says the label matters less than the benefits [^3][^4].
differences: Trump has suggested a closer Canada-EU tie could be hostile and threatened tariffs on Europe; Canadian officials say it is not aimed at the US [^4]. In Europe, an analyst says France and Germany dislike the "associate member" label [^4]. At home, Conservative critic Michelle Rempel Garner wants clarity on effects on jobs and housing [^3].
